items.title: What does a used engine cost in the UK?
items.description: The short answer: Used engines cost between £500 and £3,200 supply-only. Fitted costs range from £1,000 to £4,500 depending on engine type, mileage, and condition. The longer answer: For most UK drivers replacing a common 4-cylinder diesel or petrol engine, expect to pay £900-£2,200 supply-only for a used unit with reasonable mileage (60,000-80,000 miles). Fitting adds £800-£2,200 depending on your location and the garage you choose. Based on 7,284 real used engine quote requests processed through Engines Market in 2025 [EM-VERIFIED] , here's what UK owners are actually paying for used engines.

blocks.text: [EM-QUOTE] These figures are derived from actual supplier quotes submitted through our platform for used engines. Fitted costs assume independent specialist labour at regional average rates. Main dealer costs are typically 40-60% higher.

items.title: What does "used engine" actually mean?
items.description: Understanding what a "used engine" actually is - and what it isn't - is critical before you buy one.

blocks.text: Used engines typically come from donor vehicles with 40,000 to 120,000 miles . The mileage is usually known from the donor vehicle's odometer, but in some cases, it may be estimated.

Important: Mileage claims are not always verified. Some suppliers may not be able to confirm the exact mileage of a used engine, especially if it came from a written-off vehicle with a damaged dashboard or cluster.

blocks.text: The Labour Coverage Problem: This is the biggest hidden cost of used engine warranties. Scenario: You buy a used engine for £1,200 with a 3-month parts-only warranty. After 6 weeks, it develops a knocking noise. The supplier agrees to replace the engine under warranty. What's covered: The replacement engine (if they have one in stock). What's NOT covered: The £800-£1,500 labour cost to remove the failed engine and fit the replacement. Result: You're out of pocket for the labour, and the car is off the road again.
Our advice: Ask every supplier: "Is your warranty parts-only or parts AND labour?" Get the answer in writing.

items.title: Be brutally honest about the risks
items.description: A used engine is cheap for a reason. Here's what you need to know before buying.

cards.title: 📋 1. Unknown Service History
cards.text: Most used engines come with no documented service history. You have no way of knowing how often the oil was changed, whether the correct oil was used, or if the engine was overheated.
cards.fullText: 📋 1. Unknown Service History Most used engines come with no documented service history. You have no way of knowing how often the oil was changed, whether the correct oil was used, or if the engine was overheated.

cards.title: 🔩 2. No Upgraded Components
cards.text: A used engine uses the original parts it came with - old seals, gaskets, timing components, piston rings, and bearings that may be at end of life.
cards.fullText: 🔩 2. No Upgraded Components A used engine uses the original parts it came with - old seals, gaskets, timing components, piston rings, and bearings that may be at end of life.

cards.title: 🔍 3. Potential Hidden Damage
cards.text: Hairline cracks in the cylinder head, block porosity, borescope damage, internal wear from oil starvation - these may not show up until the engine is fitted.
cards.fullText: 🔍 3. Potential Hidden Damage Hairline cracks in the cylinder head, block porosity, borescope damage, internal wear from oil starvation - these may not show up until the engine is fitted.

cards.title: 💷 4. No Labour Warranty (The Hidden Cost)
cards.text: Even with a parts warranty, you'll almost certainly have to pay for labour again if the engine fails - adding £800-£2,200 to the cost.
cards.fullText: 💷 4. No Labour Warranty (The Hidden Cost) Even with a parts warranty, you'll almost certainly have to pay for labour again if the engine fails - adding £800-£2,200 to the cost.

cards.title: 📊 5. Mileage May Be Inaccurate
cards.text: Odometer may have been damaged in the accident that wrote off the vehicle, or the cluster may have been swapped. You could be paying a premium for higher mileage.
cards.fullText: 📊 5. Mileage May Be Inaccurate Odometer may have been damaged in the accident that wrote off the vehicle, or the cluster may have been swapped. You could be paying a premium for higher mileage.

cards.title: ⚙️ 6. Ancillary Components Are Still Old
cards.text: Alternator, starter, injectors, turbo, pumps - if they fail shortly after fitting, you'll pay labour again.
cards.fullText: ⚙️ 6. Ancillary Components Are Still Old Alternator, starter, injectors, turbo, pumps - if they fail shortly after fitting, you'll pay labour again.

cards.title: 🔌 7. Compatibility Issues
cards.text: Different ECU calibrations, emissions equipment, flywheel/clutch configurations, and sensor packages can cause problems even with the same engine code.
cards.fullText: 🔌 7. Compatibility Issues Different ECU calibrations, emissions equipment, flywheel/clutch configurations, and sensor packages can cause problems even with the same engine code.

cards.title: 🧪 8. No Testing / Poor Testing
cards.text: "Tested" can mean different things - a compression test (good), a visual inspection (minimal), a running test (best), or just "we think it works" (dangerous).
cards.fullText: 🧪 8. No Testing / Poor Testing "Tested" can mean different things - a compression test (good), a visual inspection (minimal), a running test (best), or just "we think it works" (dangerous).

items.title: 8 steps to protect yourself
items.description: If you're buying a used engine, here's what you should check before handing over any money.

cards.title: 🔢 1. Verify the Engine Code
cards.text: The engine code must match your vehicle's VIN. Even small variations (N47D20A vs N47D20C) can cause compatibility issues. Ask the supplier to confirm and cross-reference it with your VIN.
cards.fullText: 🔢 1. Verify the Engine Code The engine code must match your vehicle's VIN. Even small variations (N47D20A vs N47D20C) can cause compatibility issues. Ask the supplier to confirm and cross-reference it with your VIN.

cards.title: 📊 2. Ask for Mileage and Documentation
cards.text: Ask for documented mileage from the donor vehicle. If the supplier can't provide it, be cautious. "What's the verified mileage of this engine? Do you have documentation?"
cards.fullText: 📊 2. Ask for Mileage and Documentation Ask for documented mileage from the donor vehicle. If the supplier can't provide it, be cautious. "What's the verified mileage of this engine? Do you have documentation?"

cards.title: 📋 3. Request a Compression Test Report
cards.text: A compression test tells you the condition of the piston rings and valves. Ask for a report showing compression values for each cylinder and variation (should be within 10%).
cards.fullText: 📋 3. Request a Compression Test Report A compression test tells you the condition of the piston rings and valves. Ask for a report showing compression values for each cylinder and variation (should be within 10%).

cards.title: 🎥 4. Ask for a Running Video
cards.text: Listen for unusual noises (knocking, ticking, rattling), excessive smoke (blue = oil, white = coolant, black = fuel), and smooth idle. "Can you send a video of this engine running?"
cards.fullText: 🎥 4. Ask for a Running Video Listen for unusual noises (knocking, ticking, rattling), excessive smoke (blue = oil, white = coolant, black = fuel), and smooth idle. "Can you send a video of this engine running?"

cards.title: 🔍 5. Inspect for Visible Damage
cards.text: Check for oil leaks (main seals, valve cover, sump), coolant leaks, cracked/damaged mounting points, signs of overheating, and missing/broken ancillaries.
cards.fullText: 🔍 5. Inspect for Visible Damage Check for oil leaks (main seals, valve cover, sump), coolant leaks, cracked/damaged mounting points, signs of overheating, and missing/broken ancillaries.

cards.title: 🛡️ 6. Check the Warranty Terms
cards.text: Get the warranty terms in writing: duration, coverage (parts-only or parts + labour), exclusions, and claims process. "Can you send me your warranty terms in writing before I buy?"
cards.fullText: 🛡️ 6. Check the Warranty Terms Get the warranty terms in writing: duration, coverage (parts-only or parts + labour), exclusions, and claims process. "Can you send me your warranty terms in writing before I buy?"

cards.title: 🏢 7. Verify the Supplier
cards.text: Check the supplier is legitimate: UK registered company (Companies House number), physical business address, online reviews, and at least 12 months trading history.
cards.fullText: 🏢 7. Verify the Supplier Check the supplier is legitimate: UK registered company (Companies House number), physical business address, online reviews, and at least 12 months trading history.

cards.title: ⚙️ 8. Ask About Ancillaries
cards.text: Check what's included: alternator, starter motor, injectors, turbo, wiring loom, ECU. "What ancillaries are included with this engine?"
cards.fullText: ⚙️ 8. Ask About Ancillaries Check what's included: alternator, starter motor, injectors, turbo, wiring loom, ECU. "What ancillaries are included with this engine?"

faqs.question: How much does a used engine cost in the UK? +
faqs.answer: Used engines cost £500-£3,200 supply-only depending on engine type, mileage, and condition. Fitted costs range from £1,000 to £4,500 . Four-cylinder petrol engines are cheapest (£500-£1,500), V8 and high-performance engines are most expensive (£1,800-£3,500+).

faqs.question: Is a used engine a good idea? +
faqs.answer: A used engine is a good idea if your vehicle is worth under £5,000 and you plan to keep it for less than 12-18 months . If your vehicle is worth more than £5,000 or you plan to keep it longer, a reconditioned engine is usually better value long-term.

faqs.question: What's the difference between tested and untested? +
faqs.answer: A tested engine has been compression tested and inspected. It may have a video of it running. An untested engine has not been checked and is sold "as-is." Tested engines cost more but carry lower risk.

faqs.question: What warranty comes with a used engine? +
faqs.answer: Typically 1-6 months . Most used engine warranties are parts-only (you pay labour if it fails). Some suppliers offer parts and labour warranties for premium used engines. Always check in writing.

faqs.question: Can I fit a used engine from a different vehicle? +
faqs.answer: Yes, but you need the exact same engine code and often the same variant to ensure compatibility. Your supplier will match the engine code to your vehicle's VIN. Never assume a similar engine will fit.

faqs.question: What happens if the used engine fails after fitting? +
faqs.answer: If you have a parts warranty, the supplier will replace the engine (if available). You will almost certainly need to pay the labour cost again to remove the failed unit and fit the replacement. This is usually £800-£2,200 .

faqs.question: How do I know if a used engine has been properly tested? +
faqs.answer: Ask for a compression test report . Ask for a video of the engine running . Listen for unusual noises. If the supplier can't provide these, assume the engine hasn't been properly tested.

faqs.question: Is a used engine cheaper than a reconditioned engine? +
faqs.answer: Yes. Used engines are typically £1,500-£3,000 cheaper than reconditioned engines. However, the lower price comes with higher risk and shorter warranty.

faqs.question: What's the best mileage for a used engine? +
faqs.answer: Ideally under 80,000 miles for diesel and under 60,000 miles for petrol. However, condition and maintenance are more important than mileage alone. A well-maintained 80,000-mile engine is better than a neglected 40,000-mile engine.

faqs.question: Should I buy a used engine with high mileage? +
faqs.answer: Only if the price is significantly lower and you're willing to accept the risk. High-mileage engines (over 100,000 miles) are more likely to have worn components and hidden issues.

faqs.question: Can I negotiate the price of a used engine? +
faqs.answer: Yes. Used engines are often negotiable, especially if the supplier has had them in stock for a while. Ask if there's any flexibility on the price, especially if you're buying a used engine without ancillaries.

faqs.question: What's the most requested used engine? +
faqs.answer: The VW/Audi EA189 2.0 TDI is the most requested used engine, with 1,050 requests in 2025 [EM-VERIFIED] . The Ford DV6 1.6 TDCi is second with 780 requests.

faqs.question: What vehicles are used engines typically bought for? +
faqs.answer: 96% of used engine requests are for vehicles over 15 years old or valued at £5,000 or less [EM-VERIFIED] . Used engines are predominantly chosen for older, lower-value vehicles.

faqs.question: What should I do if the used engine fails? +
faqs.answer: Contact the supplier immediately. Follow their warranty claims process. Keep all documentation (receipt, warranty terms, communication). Be prepared to pay labour costs again if your warranty is parts-only.

faqs.question: Can I buy a used engine online? +
faqs.answer: Yes. Most used engine suppliers operate online. However, we recommend doing thorough due diligence: check reviews, verify the supplier's business registration, ask for videos and photos, and get warranty terms in writing before paying.
